questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economics is best defined as the study of how
options: scarce resources are allocated to satisfy unlimited human wants
businesses advertise their products
countries maintain diplomatic relations
governments collect taxes from citizens
questions.explanation: Economics fundamentally studies the allocation of limited (scarce) resources among competing, virtually unlimited human wants and needs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Scarcity in economics refers to the situation where
options: there is an oversupply of goods and services
prices of goods are fixed by the government
goods are deliberately withheld from the market
available resources are insufficient to satisfy all human wants
questions.explanation: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: resources (land, labour, capital) are limited relative to the unlimited wants of individuals and society.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Because of scarcity, every economic decision necessarily involves making a
options: guaranteed profit
government intervention
permanent solution to all wants
choice among competing alternatives
questions.explanation: Since resources cannot satisfy every want, individuals and societies must choose which wants to satisfy and which to forgo, a direct consequence of scarcity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Opportunity cost is best defined as the
options: profit earned from a business venture
amount of money spent on a purchase
total cost of producing a good
value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures what is sacrificed (the best alternative given up) when a particular choice is made among scarce resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A scale of preference is a list that arranges an individual's
options: wants in order of importance, from the most pressing to the least pressing
possessions by monetary value
income sources from highest to lowest
debts from largest to smallest
questions.explanation: A scale of preference helps an individual rank their many wants by priority, guiding decisions on which wants to satisfy first given limited resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following best illustrates the concept of opportunity cost?
options: A farmer plants more than one crop
A student chooses to study instead of watching a movie, giving up the enjoyment of the movie
A government prints more currency
A company increases its total revenue
questions.explanation: By choosing to study, the student forgoes the next best alternative use of that time (watching the movie), which represents the opportunity cost of studying.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Human wants are generally considered to be
options: identical for every individual
unaffected by income levels
limited and easily satisfied completely
unlimited, since satisfying one want often creates new ones
questions.explanation: A basic assumption in economics is that human wants are virtually insatiable; even after one want is satisfied, new wants tend to arise.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The basic economic problems every society must solve include deciding
options: only what price to charge for goods
only how to spend government revenue
only how much tax to collect
what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
questions.explanation: Every economic system, regardless of type, must answer these three fundamental questions given the scarcity of resources relative to wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In a capitalist (free market) economic system, economic decisions are primarily made by
options: international organisations only
the central government through central planning
a council of religious leaders
individuals and private businesses responding to market forces
questions.explanation: Capitalism relies on private ownership of resources and decisions driven by supply, demand, and price signals in free markets, with minimal government intervention.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In a socialist (command) economic system, the basic economic problems are solved mainly by
options: a completely unregulated market
religious institutions
central government planning and control of resources
the free interaction of individual buyers and sellers
questions.explanation: Socialist/command economies rely on centralized government planning to determine what, how, and for whom goods are produced, rather than market forces.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A mixed economic system is characterised by
options: the total absence of private businesses
complete government ownership of all resources
a total absence of any government regulation
a combination of both private enterprise and government intervention in economic activities
questions.explanation: Mixed economies blend elements of both capitalism and socialism, allowing private enterprise to operate alongside government regulation and public sector involvement.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One key feature of a capitalist economic system is
options: the absence of a price mechanism
state ownership of all major industries
the right to private ownership of property and means of production
central planning of all production decisions
questions.explanation: Private property rights, allowing individuals and firms to own and control resources and businesses, are a defining feature of capitalism.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Nigerian economy is generally classified as a
options: purely traditional economy
purely capitalist economy
purely socialist (command) economy
mixed economy
questions.explanation: Nigeria's economy combines private enterprise with significant government involvement and regulation in sectors such as oil, utilities, and infrastructure, making it a mixed economy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One disadvantage commonly associated with a purely socialist economic system is that it
options: guarantees the fastest possible economic growth
may reduce individual initiative and efficiency due to lack of profit motive
relies entirely on the price mechanism
always leads to extreme income inequality
questions.explanation: Because production decisions are centrally planned rather than profit-driven, socialist economies are often criticised for potentially weaker incentives for efficiency and innovation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In statistics, the arithmetic mean of a set of values is calculated as the
options: difference between the highest and lowest values
value that occurs most frequently
middle value when data is arranged in order
sum of all the values divided by the number of values
questions.explanation: The mean (average) is found by adding all data values together and dividing by the total count of values.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The median of a data set is defined as the
options: middle value when the data is arranged in ascending or descending order
most frequently occurring value
sum of all values divided by their count
difference between the largest and smallest values
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value of an ordered data set, dividing the data into two equal halves; for an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle values.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The mode of a data set refers to the
options: average of all the values
middle value of an ordered data set
range between the highest and lowest values
value that occurs most frequently in the data set
questions.explanation: The mode identifies the most commonly occurring value(s) in a data set, useful for categorical or frequently repeated numerical data.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: What is the mean of the following set of numbers: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12?

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The range of a data set is calculated as the
options: difference between the highest and lowest values
middle value of the data set
average of the highest and lowest values
sum of all the values
questions.explanation: Range = highest value - lowest value, providing a simple measure of the spread (dispersion) of a data set.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Standard deviation is a statistical measure used to indicate the
options: most frequently occurring value in a data set
total sum of all data values
degree of dispersion (spread) of data values around the mean
central tendency of a data set
questions.explanation: Standard deviation quantifies how much individual data points typically deviate from the mean, with a larger value indicating greater spread/variability.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A pie chart is most useful for representing data as
options: trends changing continuously over time
the relationship between two continuous variables
raw, unprocessed numerical data only
proportions of a whole, shown as slices of a circle
questions.explanation: Pie charts visually represent how a total quantity is divided into categorical proportions, with each slice representing a percentage of the whole.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A line graph is particularly useful in economics for showing
options: how a variable changes continuously over a period of time
the proportion of a total represented by different categories
the frequency of a single categorical value
unordered qualitative data
questions.explanation: Line graphs effectively illustrate trends and changes in a variable (e.g., price, GDP) over successive time periods, making patterns easy to observe.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of demand states that, other things being equal, as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded
options: remains constant
becomes infinite
falls
rises
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: consumers buy less of a good as its price increases, ceteris paribus.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of supply states that, other things being equal, as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied
options: becomes zero
falls
rises
remains constant
questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct (positive) relationship between price and quantity supplied: producers are willing to supply more as price increases, ceteris paribus.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where
options: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
price is at its highest possible level
questions.explanation: Equilibrium price is where the demand and supply curves intersect, at which the amount buyers wish to purchase exactly matches the amount sellers wish to sell.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A rightward shift of the demand curve (an increase in demand) can be caused by
options: an increase in the price of the good itself
an increase in the number of sellers only
a decrease in consumer income (for a normal good)
an increase in consumer income (for a normal good)
questions.explanation: For a normal good, rising consumer income increases the quantity demanded at every price level, shifting the entire demand curve to the right.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A leftward shift of the supply curve (a decrease in supply) can be caused by
options: a decrease in the price of production inputs
an improvement in production technology
an increase in the cost of production inputs
an increase in the number of firms in the market
questions.explanation: Higher input costs make production less profitable at every price level, causing producers to supply less, shifting the supply curve to the left.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If the price of a good is set above the equilibrium price, the immediate result will be
options: no change in the market
an automatic decrease in supply to zero
a shortage, as quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
a surplus, as quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
questions.explanation: At a price above equilibrium, producers are willing to supply more than consumers wish to buy, creating a surplus (excess supply) that tends to push the price back down.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If the price of a good is set below the equilibrium price, the immediate result will be
options: a shortage, as quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
a surplus, as quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
no change in the market
an automatic increase in supply to infinity
questions.explanation: At a price below equilibrium, consumers want to buy more than producers are willing to supply at that price, creating a shortage (excess demand).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Price elasticity of demand measures the
options: total revenue earned from selling a good
responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price
absolute change in price of a good
cost of producing an additional unit of a good
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand (percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price) shows how sensitive consumer purchasing is to price changes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A good is said to have elastic demand when
options: a large percentage change in price causes a smaller percentage change in quantity demanded
a small percentage change in price causes a proportionately larger percentage change in quantity demanded
quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes
the price of the good has no effect on any other good
questions.explanation: Elastic demand (elasticity greater than 1) means consumers are highly responsive to price changes, so quantity demanded changes proportionately more than price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Necessities such as salt typically have _____ demand, since consumers must buy them regardless of price changes.
options: highly elastic
inelastic
unitary elastic
perfectly elastic
questions.explanation: Goods considered necessities tend to have inelastic demand (elasticity less than 1), since consumers continue purchasing similar quantities even when price rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Complementary goods, such as bread and butter, are characterised by the fact that a rise in the price of one
options: leads to a fall in the demand for the other
has no effect whatsoever on the demand for the other
always causes both goods to disappear from the market
leads to a rise in the demand for the other
questions.explanation: Complementary goods are used together, so a price rise in one (reducing its quantity demanded) also reduces demand for the other good typically consumed alongside it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Substitute goods, such as tea and coffee, are characterised by the fact that a rise in the price of one
options: leads to a rise in the demand for the other
has no effect on the demand for the other
causes both goods to become complementary
leads to a fall in the demand for the other
questions.explanation: When the price of one substitute good rises, consumers tend to switch to the relatively cheaper alternative, increasing demand for the substitute good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Total utility refers to the
options: price paid for a unit of a good
overall satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming a given quantity of a good
cost of producing a good
additional satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good
questions.explanation: Total utility measures the entire satisfaction gained from consuming a certain total amount of a good or service, accumulating as more units are consumed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Marginal utility is defined as the
options: cost of the last unit produced
total satisfaction from all units consumed
additional satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit of a good
average price of all units consumed
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the extra utility (satisfaction) a consumer gains from consuming one additional unit of a good, beyond what was already consumed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that as a consumer consumes more units of a good,
options: the additional satisfaction gained from each successive unit tends to decrease
the additional satisfaction from each successive unit tends to increase
the price of the good automatically falls
total utility always decreases
questions.explanation: This law explains that, beyond a certain point, each extra unit of a good consumed yields progressively less additional satisfaction than the unit before it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A rational consumer aims to maximise total utility by allocating income such that the
options: cheapest good available is always purchased exclusively
entire income is spent on a single good only
most expensive good available is always purchased exclusively
marginal utility per naira spent is equal across all goods purchased
questions.explanation: Utility-maximising behaviour occurs when a consumer allocates spending so that the marginal utility obtained per unit of currency is equalised across all goods bought.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The point at which marginal utility becomes zero indicates that the consumer has reached
options: the minimum possible price for the good
zero total utility from the good
maximum total utility from consuming that good
a state where the good is no longer needed at any price
questions.explanation: Total utility is at its peak precisely when marginal utility (the addition to total utility) falls to zero; consuming further units beyond this point would begin to reduce total utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following best illustrates the Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility?
options: A firm producing more output as its costs decrease
The satisfaction gained from eating the fourth slice of bread is less than that from the first slice
A consumer buying more of a good as its price falls
A government increasing tax rates on luxury goods
questions.explanation: As successive units of the same good are consumed within a given period, each additional unit typically yields less extra satisfaction than the one before, exactly as the law describes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Fixed costs of production are costs that
options: are always higher than variable costs
vary directly and proportionately with output
only occur when output is zero
do not change with the level of output in the short run
questions.explanation: Fixed costs (e.g., rent, insurance) remain constant regardless of how much is produced in the short run, unlike variable costs, which change with output level.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Variable costs of production are costs that
options: change directly with the level of output produced
never change over the life of a business
are incurred only once, at the start of production
remain constant regardless of output level
questions.explanation: Variable costs (e.g., raw materials, hourly wages) rise and fall with the quantity of output produced, unlike fixed costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Total cost of production is calculated as the
options: difference between total fixed and total variable cost
sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost
total revenue minus total profit
average cost multiplied by fixed cost
questions.explanation: Total Cost (TC) = Total Fixed Cost (TFC) + Total Variable Cost (TVC), combining both cost components at a given output level.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Average cost of production is calculated by
options: multiplying total cost by the quantity of output
subtracting fixed cost from total cost
dividing total cost by the quantity of output produced
dividing total revenue by total cost
questions.explanation: Average cost (AC = TC/Q) shows the cost incurred per unit of output produced, a key measure for assessing production efficiency.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Marginal cost is defined as the
options: additional cost incurred from producing one more unit of output
total cost of producing all units
fixed cost divided by variable cost
average cost of production at the maximum output level
questions.explanation: Marginal cost (MC) measures the extra cost a firm incurs by producing one additional unit of output, crucial for output and pricing decisions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Law of Diminishing Returns states that as more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, eventually
options: the fixed factor becomes variable
the additional (marginal) output from each extra unit of the variable factor will decrease
output will increase indefinitely at a constant rate
total output will immediately fall to zero
questions.explanation: This law describes short-run production: beyond an optimal point, adding more of a variable input (e.g., labour) to fixed factors (e.g., land) yields progressively smaller marginal output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economies of scale refer to the
options: total cost of producing a single unit of output
fixed costs incurred regardless of firm size
reduction in average cost of production as a firm increases its scale (size) of output
increase in average cost as output rises
questions.explanation: Economies of scale occur when a firm's average cost per unit falls as it expands production, often due to specialisation, bulk purchasing, or more efficient use of resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Diseconomies of scale occur when a firm expands beyond an optimal size, resulting in
options: continuously falling average costs
rising average costs due to inefficiencies such as poor coordination and communication
constant average costs regardless of size
an automatic increase in profit
questions.explanation: Beyond a certain size, further expansion can create management and coordination difficulties, causing average costs to rise rather than continue falling.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Total revenue of a firm is calculated as
options: marginal cost multiplied by output
price per unit multiplied by the quantity of units sold
average cost multiplied by fixed cost
total cost minus total profit
questions.explanation: Total Revenue (TR) = Price (P) x Quantity sold (Q), representing the total income a firm earns from selling its output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Profit is calculated as the
options: average of total revenue and total cost
product of total revenue and total cost
sum of total revenue and total cost
difference between total revenue and total cost
questions.explanation: Profit = Total Revenue - Total Cost; a positive value indicates the firm earns more than it spends, while a negative value indicates a loss.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Perfect competition is a market structure characterised by
options: product differentiation as the main basis of competition
many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, and free entry and exit
a few large firms dominating the market
a single seller controlling the entire market
questions.explanation: Perfect competition assumes numerous small firms selling identical products, with no barriers to entering or leaving the industry, and no single firm able to influence price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A monopoly market structure exists when
options: a single firm is the sole supplier of a good or service with no close substitutes
many firms sell identical products
a few large firms dominate the market
firms compete mainly through product differentiation
questions.explanation: Monopoly describes a market dominated entirely by one seller, who therefore has significant control over price due to the absence of close substitute products.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Monopolistic competition is a market structure in which
options: only one firm supplies the entire market
a few large firms dominate through interdependent pricing decisions
products are completely identical across all sellers
many firms sell similar but slightly differentiated products
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition combines features of competition (many sellers) and monopoly (product differentiation), as firms sell similar goods marketed as distinct through branding.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An oligopoly market structure is characterised by
options: completely homogeneous products with no branding at all
an unlimited number of small firms
one firm controlling the entire supply
a small number of large firms dominating the market, often with interdependent pricing decisions
questions.explanation: In oligopoly, a few large firms dominate the industry, and each firm's decisions (especially on price) significantly affect and are affected by rivals' actions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Under perfect competition, an individual firm is considered a 'price taker' because it
options: controls the total market supply
sets its own price independently of the market
has no power to influence the market price and must accept the prevailing price
can charge different prices to different customers
questions.explanation: Since each firm in perfect competition is small relative to the whole market and sells an identical product, it must sell at the market-determined price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A key barrier to entry that helps sustain a monopoly is
options: zero fixed costs of production
the presence of many competing firms
exclusive control over a key resource, patent, or government licence
perfectly homogeneous products across the industry
questions.explanation: Monopolies are often sustained by barriers to entry such as patents, exclusive licences, or sole control of an essential resource, preventing competitors from entering the market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Price discrimination, sometimes practised by a monopolist, involves
options: charging different prices to different groups of consumers for the same product
charging the same price to all consumers regardless of circumstances
always charging the lowest possible price to all consumers
eliminating all price differences in a market
questions.explanation: Price discrimination allows a firm with market power to charge different consumer segments different prices for an identical good, maximising its revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Advertising and branding are commonly used as competitive tools mainly in which market structure?
options: Monopolistic competition
Pure monopoly with no substitutes
Perfect competition
None of these market structures
questions.explanation: Since firms in monopolistic competition sell similar products, they rely heavily on advertising and branding to differentiate their goods and attract customers.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following market structures has the largest number of buyers and sellers, with no single participant able to affect price?
options: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Monopolistic competition
Oligopoly
questions.explanation: Perfect competition, by definition, involves the greatest number of small, price-taking buyers and sellers, none of whom can individually influence market price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A cartel, sometimes formed under an oligopoly, refers to an agreement among firms to
options: collude on price and output levels to reduce competition among themselves
merge into a single large monopoly firm
eliminate all forms of advertising
compete aggressively on price to gain market share
questions.explanation: A cartel is a formal or informal agreement among typically oligopolistic firms to coordinate pricing and output, effectively reducing competition and behaving somewhat like a monopoly.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is defined as the total value of
options: all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period
government spending alone in a fiscal year
goods and services produced by a country's citizens abroad only
raw materials extracted from a country
questions.explanation: GDP measures the market value of all final goods and services produced domestically (within the country's borders) over a specific time period, usually a year.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Gross National Product (GNP) differs from GDP mainly in that GNP includes
options: only domestic production within the country's borders
only exports and excludes all imports
income earned by a country's citizens both domestically and abroad, but excludes income earned by foreigners within the country
only government expenditure
questions.explanation: GNP measures output produced by a nation's citizens and businesses regardless of location, while GDP measures output produced within the country's borders regardless of nationality.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Net National Product (NNP) is obtained by
options: adding depreciation to Gross National Product
subtracting depreciation (capital consumption) from Gross National Product
subtracting exports from Gross National Product
adding government transfer payments to GDP
questions.explanation: NNP = GNP - Depreciation, accounting for the wearing out of capital equipment during the production process over the period measured.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a common method of measuring national income?
options: Only the population census method
Only the import-export method
The income method, output method, and expenditure method
Only the taxation method
questions.explanation: National income can be estimated using three approaches: summing incomes earned, summing the value of output produced, or summing total expenditure, which should theoretically yield the same total.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The circular flow of income model illustrates the
options: process of setting the exchange rate
flow of exports and imports between two countries
flow of income and expenditure between households and firms in an economy
structure of a country's banking system alone
questions.explanation: The circular flow model shows how households supply factors of production to firms in exchange for income, which they then spend on goods and services produced by those firms.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Per capita income is calculated by
options: subtracting the population from national income
multiplying national income by the population
dividing the government budget by national income
dividing a country's total national income by its total population
questions.explanation: Per capita income (national income / population) provides an average measure of income per person, often used as a rough indicator of living standards.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following would be excluded when calculating a country's GDP to avoid double counting?
options: The value of final consumer goods
Exports of finished manufactured goods
The value of intermediate goods used up in producing final goods
Government spending on public services
questions.explanation: Only final goods and services are counted in GDP; including the value of intermediate goods (already embedded in the price of final goods) would result in double counting.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Money performs several key functions, including serving as a
options: form of agricultural produce
type of tax levied by government
physical raw material for industry
medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account
questions.explanation: Money's core functions include facilitating trade (medium of exchange), preserving value over time (store of value), and providing a common measure of value (unit of account).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Before the introduction of money, trade was conducted mainly through
options: electronic bank transfers
the use of cheques
credit cards
the barter system, involving direct exchange of goods for goods
questions.explanation: Barter, the direct exchange of goods and services without money, was the primary trading method before money was introduced, but it suffered from the problem of the 'double coincidence of wants'.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Central Bank of a country is primarily responsible for
options: setting the retail prices of all goods
regulating the money supply and overseeing the banking system
collecting personal income tax directly from workers
manufacturing consumer goods for export
questions.explanation: A country's central bank (e.g., the Central Bank of Nigeria) controls monetary policy, regulates commercial banks, and manages the overall money supply and currency stability.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Commercial banks primarily function to
options: accept deposits from customers and provide loans and other banking services
regulate international trade agreements
print the national currency
set national fiscal policy
questions.explanation: Commercial banks serve as intermediaries between savers and borrowers, taking deposits and extending credit (loans) to individuals and businesses, unlike the central bank, which regulates the whole system.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Inflation is best defined as a
options: one-time increase in the price of a single good
persistent and sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services
fixed exchange rate policy
fall in the general price level over time
questions.explanation: Inflation refers to an ongoing, generalised increase in prices across an economy over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Demand-pull inflation occurs mainly when
options: the government reduces the money supply
aggregate demand in the economy exceeds the available aggregate supply
there is a sudden increase in unemployment
the cost of production inputs rises significantly
questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation arises when total spending in an economy outpaces the economy's capacity to produce goods and services, pushing prices upward.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Cost-push inflation occurs mainly when
options: the government increases interest rates
rising costs of production, such as wages or raw materials, push up the general price level
aggregate demand falls sharply
the exchange rate strengthens significantly
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation results from increased costs of production (e.g., wage rises, raw material price increases), which firms pass on to consumers as higher prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a common measure taken by a central bank to control inflation?
options: Lowering interest rates to encourage more borrowing
Removing all taxes on imported goods
Raising interest rates to reduce borrowing and spending
Increasing government subsidies on all goods
questions.explanation: Central banks often raise interest rates during inflationary periods to discourage borrowing and spending, cooling down aggregate demand and easing upward pressure on prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Deflation refers to a sustained
options: rise in the general price level of goods and services
increase in government expenditure
increase in the exchange rate of a currency
fall in the general price level of goods and services
questions.explanation: Deflation is the opposite of inflation: a persistent decrease in the overall price level in an economy, which can also cause economic difficulties like reduced spending.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The demand for money to carry out everyday transactions is known as the
options: investment motive for holding bonds
precautionary motive against inflation only
speculative motive for holding money
transactionary motive for holding money
questions.explanation: Keynes identified the transactionary motive as the need to hold money to cover routine, planned day-to-day purchases and expenses.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Public finance is the branch of economics concerned with the
options: personal savings decisions of households
trade agreements between two private companies
revenue, expenditure, and debt management of government
profit-making activities of private firms
questions.explanation: Public finance studies how governments raise revenue (mainly through taxation), spend it on public goods and services, and manage public debt.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A major source of government revenue in most economies is
options: personal loans from citizens
taxation
private charitable donations
foreign remittances from individuals
questions.explanation: Taxation, in its various forms (income tax, VAT, customs duties, etc.), is typically the largest and most reliable source of revenue for national governments.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A balanced government budget occurs when
options: government expenditure exceeds government revenue
the government has no revenue at all
government revenue equals government expenditure
government revenue exceeds government expenditure
questions.explanation: A balanced budget is achieved when total planned government spending exactly matches total planned government revenue over a fiscal period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget deficit occurs when
options: government revenue equals government expenditure
the government eliminates all forms of spending
government revenue exceeds government expenditure
government expenditure exceeds government revenue
questions.explanation: A deficit budget arises when planned government spending is greater than the revenue collected, often requiring the government to borrow to cover the shortfall.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A budget surplus occurs when
options: government revenue exceeds government expenditure
government revenue equals government expenditure
government expenditure exceeds government revenue
the government has zero revenue
questions.explanation: A surplus budget occurs when the government collects more revenue than it spends within a given fiscal period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Public debt refers to the
options: total income earned by government employees
total taxes collected by a government in a year
total value of goods exported by a country
total amount of money owed by a government to domestic and foreign creditors
questions.explanation: Public debt represents the accumulated borrowing a government has undertaken, often to finance budget deficits, owed to both local and international lenders.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The theory of absolute advantage states that a country should specialise in producing goods it can produce
options: using the most expensive available technology
only for its own domestic consumption
more efficiently (using fewer resources) than other countries
at exactly the same efficiency as other countries
questions.explanation: Adam Smith's theory of absolute advantage suggests countries benefit from trade by specialising in goods they can produce using fewer resources than their trading partners.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The theory of comparative advantage suggests that a country should specialise in producing goods for which it has the
options: highest opportunity cost among all its industries
largest absolute advantage over all trading partners
government subsidy support only
lowest opportunity cost compared to other countries, even without an absolute advantage
questions.explanation: David Ricardo's comparative advantage theory shows that countries gain from trade by specialising in goods where their opportunity cost is relatively lowest, even if they have no absolute advantage in anything.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The balance of trade refers to the difference between a country's
options: total savings and total investment
total value of exports and total value of imports of goods
money supply and demand for money
government revenue and government expenditure
questions.explanation: The balance of trade specifically measures the difference between the value of a country's merchandise exports and imports over a period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A favourable balance of trade occurs when a country's
options: exports exceed its imports
imports exceed its exports
government budget is balanced
exports equal its imports exactly
questions.explanation: A trade surplus (favourable balance of trade) exists when the value of a country's exports is greater than the value of its imports.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The balance of payments is a broader record than the balance of trade because it includes
options: only stock market transactions
all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world, including trade, services, and capital flows
only the trade in physical merchandise goods
only government-to-government financial aid
questions.explanation: The balance of payments records all economic transactions with the rest of the world, encompassing the trade balance plus services, income flows, and capital/financial account movements.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An exchange rate is best defined as the
options: tax rate imposed on imported goods
interest rate set by a country's central bank
price of one country's currency expressed in terms of another currency
total value of a country's exports
questions.explanation: The exchange rate specifies how much of one currency must be given up to obtain a unit of another currency, essential for international trade and finance.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: ECOWAS (Economic Community of West African States) was established mainly to promote
options: military alliances among European nations
trade exclusively between Nigeria and the United States
economic cooperation and integration among West African countries
the standardisation of global currencies
questions.explanation: ECOWAS is a regional economic organisation aimed at fostering trade, economic integration, and cooperation among its member states in West Africa.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) primarily assists member countries by
options: directly managing member countries' agricultural sectors
manufacturing goods for export on behalf of member states
providing financial assistance and policy advice to promote monetary cooperation and economic stability
setting domestic tax rates for its member countries
questions.explanation: The IMF works to foster global monetary cooperation, financial stability, and sustainable economic growth, often providing loans and policy guidance to countries facing balance of payments difficulties.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The World Bank primarily focuses on providing
options: military support to developing nations
long-term loans and financial/technical assistance for development projects in member countries
direct cash transfers to individual citizens
short-term currency stabilisation loans only
questions.explanation: Unlike the IMF's focus on monetary stability, the World Bank primarily funds long-term development projects (infrastructure, education, health) in developing countries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Historically, before the discovery of oil, the mainstay of the Nigerian economy was
options: information technology services
agriculture
petroleum
manufacturing of automobiles
questions.explanation: Prior to the oil boom, Nigeria's economy relied heavily on agricultural exports such as cocoa, groundnut, palm oil, and cotton for foreign exchange and employment.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a major problem currently facing agriculture in Nigeria?
options: Reliance on outdated farming methods and inadequate infrastructure
Overproduction of food crops beyond domestic and export needs
Excessive government funding for agricultural research
Too many young people going into farming
questions.explanation: Nigerian agriculture continues to be hampered by traditional farming techniques, poor rural infrastructure (roads, storage), and limited access to modern inputs and credit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Industrialization refers to the process by which an economy transforms from being primarily
options: monetary to purely barter-based
service-based to purely agricultural
agrarian to one dominated by manufacturing and industrial activities
industrial to primarily agricultural
questions.explanation: Industrialization describes the structural shift of an economy from reliance on agriculture toward greater manufacturing and industrial production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is a significant challenge to industrialization in Nigeria?
options: Complete absence of raw materials nationwide
Overregulation preventing any foreign investment whatsoever
Inadequate and unreliable power (electricity) supply
Excess availability of skilled industrial labour
questions.explanation: Unreliable electricity supply significantly raises production costs and discourages both local and foreign investment in Nigerian manufacturing industries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Population growth in Nigeria presents an economic challenge mainly because it can lead to
options: a permanent reduction in the labour force
a decrease in the demand for goods and services
pressure on limited resources, unemployment, and strain on social infrastructure
an automatic and immediate rise in per capita income
questions.explanation: Rapid population growth, if not matched by corresponding economic growth, can strain available resources, increase unemployment, and overburden schools, hospitals, and other infrastructure.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The labour market in Nigeria is often characterised by
options: an absence of any informal sector employment
guaranteed full employment for all job seekers
a persistent shortage of available workers in all sectors
a high rate of unemployment and underemployment, especially among youths
questions.explanation: Nigeria faces significant challenges of unemployment and underemployment, particularly affecting young graduates, due to a mismatch between labour supply and available formal jobs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Diversification of the Nigerian economy refers to efforts to
options: reduce dependence on oil revenue by developing other sectors such as agriculture and manufacturing
eliminate the agricultural sector entirely
focus exclusively on the service sector
increase the country's reliance solely on crude oil exports
questions.explanation: Economic diversification aims to broaden Nigeria's revenue base beyond oil by strengthening other productive sectors, reducing vulnerability to oil price shocks.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The informal sector of the Nigerian economy typically consists of
options: large multinational corporations only
publicly listed companies on the stock exchange
small-scale, often unregistered businesses and self-employed workers operating outside formal regulation
government ministries and parastatals
questions.explanation: The informal sector includes small traders, artisans, and self-employed individuals who typically operate without formal registration, taxation, or regulatory oversight, but who provide significant employment.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A country's Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) shows that to produce 20 more units of food, it must give up 20 units of cloth (moving from 100 cloth/0 food to 80 cloth/20 food). The opportunity cost of the first 20 units of food produced is
options: 100 units of cloth
0 units of cloth, since resources are unlimited
80 units of cloth
20 units of cloth
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is measured by what is given up; here, producing 20 units of food required sacrificing 20 units of cloth (100-80).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The typical concave (bowed-out) shape of a Production Possibility Frontier illustrates the
options: law of increasing opportunity cost as more of one good is produced
principle of absolute advantage
law of demand
law of diminishing marginal utility
questions.explanation: The concave shape reflects that resources are not perfectly adaptable between uses, so producing successive units of one good requires giving up increasing amounts of the other good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A point lying inside (below) a country's Production Possibility Frontier indicates that the economy is
options: producing at maximum attainable efficiency
producing an output combination that is currently unattainable
exporting more than it imports
experiencing unemployment or underutilisation of resources
questions.explanation: Points inside the PPF represent inefficient use of available resources, such as unemployed labour or idle capital, since more of both goods could be produced.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An outward shift of an entire Production Possibility Frontier is most likely caused by
options: an increase in unemployment
an improvement in technology or an increase in available resources
a fall in consumer income
a rise in the price of one of the two goods produced
questions.explanation: An outward shift represents economic growth in productive capacity, typically resulting from technological advancement or a growth in the quantity/quality of factors of production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a scale of preference from opportunity cost?
options: Opportunity cost ranks wants, while a scale of preference measures forgone alternatives
A scale of preference ranks wants in order of urgency, while opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone in satisfying the top want
They are identical concepts with no difference
Both concepts apply only to government budgeting
questions.explanation: A scale of preference is a ranked list of wants, whereas opportunity cost specifically refers to what is sacrificed when a choice from that list is made.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The statement 'the government should reduce fuel subsidy to save more money' is an example of
options: normative economics, since it expresses an opinion or value judgement
a purely descriptive statistical statement
a positive economic statement
a law of supply
questions.explanation: Normative economics deals with value judgements about what 'should' happen, unlike positive economics, which deals with objective, testable facts.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following correctly matches a factor of production with its reward?
options: Land - profit; Capital - wages
Labour - rent; Land - wages
Capital - interest; Entrepreneur - profit
Entrepreneur - rent; Labour - interest
questions.explanation: The conventional rewards to factors of production are: land - rent, labour - wages, capital - interest, and entrepreneur - profit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In answering the basic economic question of 'for whom to produce', an economy is essentially deciding
options: which technology to adopt
how to advertise finished goods
what quantity of goods to import
how goods and services should be distributed among members of society
questions.explanation: 'For whom to produce' concerns the distribution of the output produced among the members of society, based on income, needs, or government policy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of a free enterprise (capitalist) economic system?
options: Private ownership of the means of production
Profit as the main motive for production
Freedom of choice for consumers and producers
Government fixing of prices for virtually all goods and services
questions.explanation: Widespread government price-fixing across virtually all goods is characteristic of a command economy, not a free enterprise system, which relies on market-determined prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A key weakness often associated with pure central planning, compared with a market economy, is that it
options: responds more quickly to changes in consumer tastes than markets do
guarantees zero unemployment in all circumstances
eliminates the need for economic decision-making entirely
tends to be slower in responding to changing consumer demand due to the absence of price signals
questions.explanation: Without a functioning price mechanism to signal changes in demand and supply, centrally planned economies often adjust output more slowly and less efficiently than market economies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The price of a good rises from N20 to N25, and the quantity demanded falls from 100 units to 80 units. The price elasticity of demand is approximately
options: 1.25 (elastic)
0.8 (inelastic)
0.2 (perfectly inelastic)
2.0 (elastic)
questions.explanation: Percentage change in quantity = -20/100 = -20%; percentage change in price = 5/20 = 25%. PED = -20%/25% = -0.8, indicating inelastic demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Given the demand function Qd = 100 - 2P and the supply function Qs = 20 + 3P, the equilibrium price and quantity are
questions.explanation: Setting Qd = Qs: 100 - 2P = 20 + 3P gives 80 = 5P, so P = 16; substituting gives Q = 100 - 2(16) = 68.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If a rise in the price of good A causes an increase in the demand for good B, then goods A and B are best described as
options: inferior goods, with a negative income elasticity of demand
independent goods, with zero cross elasticity of demand
substitute goods, with a positive cross elasticity of demand
complementary goods, with a negative cross elasticity of demand
questions.explanation: A positive cross elasticity of demand (quantity demanded of B rises when price of A rises) indicates that A and B are substitutes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: When the price of a good falls and, as a result, the quantity demanded of that same good rises along an unchanged demand curve, this is correctly called
options: a shift of the demand curve
an extension (movement along) of demand
an increase in demand
a decrease in demand
questions.explanation: A change in quantity demanded due solely to a change in the good's own price is a movement along the existing demand curve, known as an extension or contraction, not a shift.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The price of a good rises from N50 to N60, and the quantity supplied rises from 200 to 260 units. The price elasticity of supply is
options: 1.0 (unitary)
2.0 (elastic)
0.67 (inelastic)
1.5 (elastic)
questions.explanation: Percentage change in quantity supplied = 60/200 = 30%; percentage change in price = 10/50 = 20%. PES = 30%/20% = 1.5, indicating elastic supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A Giffen good is unusual because
options: it is always a luxury good with high income elasticity
a fall in its price leads to a decrease in the quantity demanded, defying the ordinary law of demand
it has zero price elasticity of demand at every price
its demand curve slopes downward like a normal good
questions.explanation: A Giffen good violates the law of demand: as its price falls, the strong negative income effect for very poor consumers causes quantity demanded to fall rather than rise.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A government subsidy paid to producers of a good will most likely cause the
options: demand curve to shift right, raising equilibrium quantity
supply curve to shift left, raising equilibrium price
supply curve to shift right, lowering equilibrium price and raising equilibrium quantity
demand curve to shift left, lowering equilibrium quantity
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers producers' effective cost of production, increasing supply at every price, which shifts the supply curve rightward, lowering price and raising the equilibrium quantity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Given Qd = 200 - 2P and Qs = 50 + 3P, if the government imposes a price ceiling of N20 (below the free-market equilibrium), the resulting shortage will be
options: 110 units
160 units
30 units
50 units
questions.explanation: At P = 20, Qd = 200 - 40 = 160 and Qs = 50 + 60 = 110; the shortage equals Qd - Qs = 160 - 110 = 50 units.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If demand for a good is price elastic, a reduction in its price will cause total revenue to
options: increase, since the percentage rise in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage fall in price
become zero immediately
fall, since less is being charged per unit
remain exactly unchanged
questions.explanation: With elastic demand, quantity demanded increases proportionately more than the price falls, so total revenue (price x quantity) rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An increase in consumer income causing the entire demand curve for a normal good to shift rightward is correctly termed
options: an extension of demand
a contraction of demand
a decrease in demand
an increase in demand
questions.explanation: A shift of the whole demand curve, caused by a factor other than the good's own price (such as income), is called an increase or decrease in demand, not a movement along the curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The demand for a good and its complementary good, such as cars and petrol, purchased together to satisfy one want, is an example of
options: composite demand
joint demand
derived demand
competitive demand
questions.explanation: Joint demand occurs when two or more goods are demanded together because they are used in conjunction with one another, such as cars and petrol.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes cardinal utility from ordinal utility?
options: Cardinal utility assumes satisfaction can be measured numerically in units (utils), while ordinal utility only ranks preferences without assigning numbers
Ordinal utility measures satisfaction in numerical units, while cardinal utility only ranks preferences
Both approaches assume utility cannot be compared across goods
Cardinal utility applies only to producers, while ordinal utility applies only to consumers
questions.explanation: Cardinal utility theory assumes utility is quantifiable (e.g., in 'utils'), whereas ordinal utility theory (used in indifference curve analysis) assumes consumers can only rank bundles by preference, not measure satisfaction numerically.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An indifference curve, used in ordinal utility analysis, represents
options: the market price of two goods over time
the maximum income a consumer can spend on goods
combinations of two goods yielding equal levels of a consumer's satisfaction
the exact numerical utility value obtained from a single good
questions.explanation: An indifference curve shows all combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same total level of satisfaction, without requiring utility to be numerically measured.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A consumer buys good X (Px = N5) with marginal utility of 20 utils, and good Y (Py = N8) with marginal utility of 32 utils. Based on the equi-marginal principle, the consumer is
options: not in equilibrium, and should buy more of Y
in equilibrium, since marginal utility per naira spent is equal for both goods
unable to reach equilibrium with these two goods
not in equilibrium, and should buy more of X
questions.explanation: MUx/Px = 20/5 = 4 and MUy/Py = 32/8 = 4; since both ratios are equal, the consumer is maximising total utility and is in equilibrium.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A consumer is willing to pay up to N500 for a pair of shoes but only pays the market price of N350. The consumer surplus obtained is
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what they actually pay: N500 - N350 = N150.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A consumer's marginal utility from successive units of a good is: 10, 8, 6, 3, -2. Total utility begins to fall
options: after the 5th unit, since marginal utility only becomes negative there
it never falls, since total utility always increases
after the 3rd unit
after the 2nd unit
questions.explanation: Total utility rises as long as marginal utility is positive; it only starts to fall once marginal utility becomes negative, which occurs at the 5th unit (-2).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The law of equi-marginal utility differs from the law of diminishing marginal utility in that it
options: describes how a rational consumer allocates a fixed income across goods to equalise marginal utility per naira, rather than describing the decline in utility from consuming more of one good
applies only to producers, not consumers
states that marginal utility always increases with consumption
is simply another name for the same law
questions.explanation: The law of diminishing marginal utility explains why successive units of one good yield less satisfaction, while the equi-marginal (or substitution) principle explains how income is allocated among several goods to maximise total utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Indifference curves representing consistent consumer preferences cannot intersect each other because
options: intersection would violate the assumption of transitivity of preferences, leading to a logical contradiction
intersection would imply the consumer's preferences are transitive
consumers only ever consider a single good at a time
curves are always drawn as straight lines
questions.explanation: If two indifference curves crossed, it would imply inconsistent rankings of the same bundles of goods, contradicting the basic assumption that consumer preferences are transitive and consistent.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The slope of a consumer's budget line is equal to
options: the negative of the ratio of the price of the good on the horizontal axis to the price of the good on the vertical axis
the ratio of total utility to income
the marginal utility of the two goods
the consumer's total income
questions.explanation: The budget line's slope, -Px/Py, reflects the rate at which the market allows a consumer to trade off one good for another given fixed prices and income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm's total variable cost is N600 when it produces 50 units of output. Its average variable cost is
questions.explanation: Average variable cost = Total Variable Cost / Quantity = 600 / 50 = N12.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm's total cost is N200 at 4 units of output and N250 at 5 units of output. The marginal cost of producing the 5th unit is
questions.explanation: Marginal cost equals the change in total cost from producing one more unit: N250 - N200 = N50.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm has total fixed costs of N1,000 and produces 20 units of output. Its average fixed cost is
questions.explanation: Average fixed cost = Total Fixed Cost / Quantity = 1,000 / 20 = N50.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm's break-even point occurs at the level of output where
options: total revenue equals total cost, so the firm earns exactly normal profit
total revenue exceeds total cost by the maximum amount
average fixed cost equals average variable cost
marginal cost equals marginal revenue only
questions.explanation: At the break-even point, total revenue equals total cost, meaning the firm makes zero economic (abnormal) profit but still covers all costs, earning only normal profit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm sells 10 units at N100 each (TR = N1,000) and 11 units at N95 each (TR = N1,045). The marginal revenue of the 11th unit is
questions.explanation: Marginal revenue equals the change in total revenue from selling one more unit: N1,045 - N1,000 = N45.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A profit-maximising firm, regardless of the market structure it operates in, will produce at the level of output where
options: average revenue equals average cost
average cost is at its lowest possible point
total revenue is at its absolute maximum
marginal cost equals marginal revenue
questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR); producing beyond this point would add more to cost than to revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: According to the law of variable proportions, a rational firm should ideally operate in the stage where
options: Stage III, where marginal product is negative and total product is falling
none of the three stages, since output should always be zero
Stage II, where marginal product is positive but diminishing
Stage I, where marginal product is still rising
questions.explanation: Stage II, where marginal returns are diminishing but still positive, is the economically rational range of production, balancing output against the cost of the variable factor.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The long run in production theory is best defined as the period in which
options: all factors of production are variable, with none fixed
only fixed costs can be adjusted
only labour can be varied while capital remains fixed
output cannot be changed at all
questions.explanation: In the long run, a firm can adjust all its factors of production, including capital and plant size, unlike the short run, where at least one factor is fixed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm's total cost is N800 at an output of 40 units. Its average cost is
questions.explanation: Average cost = Total Cost / Quantity = 800 / 40 = N20.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economies of scale that arise specifically from a firm's own internal expansion, such as bulk-buying discounts, are called
options: internal economies of scale
external economies of scale
diseconomies of scale
economies of scope only
questions.explanation: Internal economies of scale arise from a firm's own growth (e.g., bulk purchasing, specialisation), as opposed to external economies, which benefit an entire industry (e.g., improved regional infrastructure).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A firm earns total revenue of N15,000 and incurs total cost of N12,000. Its profit is
questions.explanation: Profit = Total Revenue - Total Cost = N15,000 - N12,000 = N3,000.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Increasing returns to scale in the long run should be distinguished from the short-run law of diminishing returns in that returns to scale describe
options: only price changes in a monopoly market
output changes when all factors of production are varied proportionately in the long run, while diminishing returns describe short-run output changes with one factor fixed
only what happens to fixed costs in the short run
the same phenomenon, just under a different name
questions.explanation: Returns to scale relate to long-run changes in output when all inputs are increased together, while diminishing returns (law of variable proportions) apply in the short run when only a variable factor changes against a fixed factor.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A key difference between the demand curve facing a perfectly competitive firm and that facing a monopolist is that the
options: both firms face identical, perfectly inelastic demand curves
perfectly competitive firm can set any price it wishes, unlike the monopolist
monopolist faces a horizontal demand curve, while the perfectly competitive firm faces a downward-sloping curve
perfectly competitive firm faces a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve at the market price, while the monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve
questions.explanation: Because a perfectly competitive firm is a price taker, it can sell any quantity at the going market price (horizontal demand), while a monopolist, being the only supplier, faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A monopolist finds that at an output of 100 units, marginal cost is N50 and marginal revenue is N50, while at 101 units marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue. The profit-maximising output is
options: 100 units
150 units
greater than 101 units
0 units
questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where MC = MR; since this occurs at 100 units, and producing beyond this point would make MC exceed MR (reducing profit), 100 units is optimal.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which pairing correctly matches a market structure with its defining feature?
options: Monopoly - many sellers offering slightly differentiated products
Oligopoly - a single seller with no substitutes
Perfect competition - a few large interdependent firms
Monopolistic competition - many sellers offering similar but differentiated products
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition is defined by many sellers offering products that are similar but differentiated (e.g., through branding), distinguishing it from monopoly, oligopoly, and perfect competition.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The kinked demand curve model is used to explain why, in an oligopoly, firms often
options: face a perfectly elastic demand curve
exhibit price rigidity, since rivals are assumed to match price cuts but not price increases
change prices very frequently in response to minor cost changes
always merge to form a single monopoly
questions.explanation: The kinked demand curve suggests oligopolists avoid changing prices because rivals would follow a price cut (losing the benefit) but not follow a price rise (losing market share), creating price stability.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A natural monopoly typically arises in an industry where
options: substantial economies of scale make it most efficient for a single firm to supply the entire market, as in utilities
there are very low barriers to entry for new firms
many small firms can compete effectively at low cost
products are highly differentiated through branding
questions.explanation: Natural monopolies (e.g., electricity or water distribution) occur where large fixed costs and economies of scale mean that a single large producer can supply the market more cheaply than multiple competing firms.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Price leadership, sometimes observed in an oligopoly, occurs when
options: all firms independently set identical prices by coincidence
firms compete only through non-price methods such as advertising
the government fixes prices for the entire industry
a dominant firm sets the price and other firms in the industry follow suit
questions.explanation: Price leadership is a form of tacit collusion where a dominant or established firm sets the price, and smaller rival firms adjust their own prices to match it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In the long-run equilibrium of a perfectly competitive market, firms earn only normal profit because
options: firms collude to fix a common price above cost
barriers to entry prevent new firms from joining the industry
price equals marginal cost, which equals the minimum point of the average cost curve
the government subsidises all firms equally
questions.explanation: Free entry and exit in perfect competition erode any supernormal profit until price equals marginal cost and minimum average cost, leaving firms with only normal profit in the long run.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Unlike a firm in perfect competition, a monopolist can continue to earn supernormal (abnormal) profit even in the long run mainly because
options: monopolists are legally required to reinvest all profits
monopoly products are always cheaper than competitive products
monopolists always operate at the lowest point of their average cost curve
barriers to entry prevent new firms from entering the market to compete away the excess profit
questions.explanation: Because entry barriers (patents, licences, control of resources) block new competitors, a monopolist can sustain supernormal profits in the long run, unlike firms in perfectly competitive markets.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: In the long-run equilibrium of monopolistic competition, firms typically operate with
options: output exactly at the minimum point of the average cost curve, as in perfect competition
a completely homogeneous product identical to all rivals
zero economic profit and excess (idle) capacity, producing below the output that minimises average cost
permanent supernormal profit protected by high barriers to entry
questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition, free entry drives economic profit to zero in the long run, but because the demand curve is downward-sloping (due to differentiation), firms produce at a point with excess capacity, below the minimum-cost output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A monopolist sells 5 units at N40 each (TR = N200) and 6 units at N35 each (TR = N210). The marginal revenue of the 6th unit is
questions.explanation: Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue: N210 - N200 = N10, illustrating why a monopolist's marginal revenue falls below price as output rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: When a monopolist charges each individual consumer the maximum price that consumer is willing to pay, this is known as
options: uniform pricing
third-degree price discrimination
first-degree (perfect) price discrimination
predatory pricing
questions.explanation: First-degree price discrimination involves charging each consumer their exact maximum willingness to pay, allowing the seller to capture the entire consumer surplus as revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The four-firm concentration ratio, often used to measure the degree of oligopoly in an industry, indicates the
options: combined market share of the four largest firms in the industry
total government tax revenue from the industry
average profit earned by all firms in the industry
total number of firms operating in an industry
questions.explanation: The concentration ratio measures what proportion of total industry output or sales is accounted for by the largest few firms (commonly four), with a high ratio indicating an oligopolistic market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Using the expenditure approach, if C = N500m, I = N150m, G = N200m, exports (X) = N100m, and imports (M) = N80m, GDP is
options: N850m
N870m
N950m
N930m

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Using the income approach, if wages = N300m, rent = N50m, interest = N40m, and profit = N110m, national income is
options: N450m
N600m
N500m
N400m
questions.explanation: National income by the income method sums all factor incomes: 300 + 50 + 40 + 110 = N500m.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A country's GDP is N800bn, and its net factor income from abroad is +N30bn. Its GNP is
options: N30bn
N830bn
N800bn
N770bn
questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad = 800 + 30 = N830bn.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A country's NNP at market price is N900bn. Indirect taxes total N80bn and subsidies total N20bn. NNP at factor cost is
options: N800bn
N840bn
N960bn
questions.explanation: NNP at factor cost = NNP at market price - indirect taxes + subsidies = 900 - 80 + 20 = N840bn.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Nominal GDP is N1,000bn and the GDP deflator is 125. Real GDP is
options: N875bn
N800bn
questions.explanation: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) x 100 = (1,000 / 125) x 100 = N800bn.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Nominal GDP is N660bn and real GDP is N600bn. The GDP deflator is
questions.explanation: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) x 100 = (660 / 600) x 100 = 110.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: National income figures in many developing countries are considered unreliable mainly because
options: a large informal and subsistence sector produces goods and services that are not officially recorded
developed countries refuse to share statistical methods
governments deliberately overstate figures every year
all transactions are conducted using foreign currency
questions.explanation: Substantial non-monetised, informal, or subsistence economic activity often goes unrecorded in official statistics, leading to understatement of true national income in many developing economies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Transfer payments, such as pensions and unemployment benefits, are excluded when calculating national income because they
options: are counted twice under the expenditure method
are always paid in foreign currency
are illegal in most countries
represent a redistribution of existing income rather than payment for newly produced goods or services
questions.explanation: Transfer payments do not correspond to any current production of goods or services; they merely redistribute income, so including them would overstate national output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: If a country records a positive net factor income from abroad, then, all else equal,
options: GNP will exceed GDP
NNP will exceed GNP
GNP will be less than GDP
GDP and GNP must always be equal
questions.explanation: Since GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad, a positive net factor income means citizens/firms earn more abroad (net) than foreigners earn domestically, making GNP greater than GDP.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Counting both the value of flour sold to a baker and the value of the bread the baker sells to consumers, without adjustment, in national income would result in
options: a negative national income figure
an accurate measure of national income
double counting, which is avoided by using the value-added method
an understatement of national income
questions.explanation: Including the value of intermediate goods (flour) alongside the final good (bread) double counts output; the value-added method avoids this by only summing the value added at each stage of production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A country's national income is N2,000,000,000 and its population is 20,000,000. Its per capita income is
questions.explanation: Per capita income = National Income / Population = 2,000,000,000 / 20,000,000 = N100.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A farmer sells wheat worth N50 to a miller, who processes it into flour and sells it for N80 to a baker, who bakes bread and sells it for N150 to consumers. Using the value-added method, the total contribution to national income from this chain is
options: N150, matching the final value of the bread
N280 (50+80+150 summed directly)
