questions.explanation: Value added at each stage (50 + 30 + 70 = 150) equals the final market value of the bread, confirming that the value-added method avoids double counting intermediate transactions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Using the Quantity Theory of Money, MV = PT, if the money supply (M) is N200m, velocity of circulation (V) is 5, and the volume of transactions (T) is 1,000 units, the general price level (P) is
questions.explanation: P = MV / T = (200,000,000 x 5) / 1,000 = 1,000,000,000 / 1,000 = 1,000, giving the average price level per transaction.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Narrow money (M1) differs from broad money (M2) in that M1 consists mainly of
options: long-term government bonds only
only foreign currency reserves
currency in circulation and demand deposits, while M2 additionally includes savings and time deposits
physical gold and other commodities
questions.explanation: M1 (narrow money) includes only the most liquid forms of money (cash and demand/current account deposits), while M2 (broad money) adds less liquid forms such as savings and time deposits.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Legal tender money is best described as currency that
options: must be accepted by law in settlement of a debt within a country
is issued exclusively by commercial banks
can only be used for international trade
has intrinsic commodity value equal to its face value
questions.explanation: Legal tender status means that a currency must, by law, be accepted as a means of settling debts within the issuing country, regardless of its intrinsic material value.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) was 150 in 2024 and rose to 165 in 2025. The rate of inflation between the two years was

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A sharp rise in global crude oil prices that increases the cost of production for firms across an economy, pushing up the general price level, is an example of
options: cost-push inflation
demand-pull inflation
structural unemployment
imported deflation
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation results from rising production costs (such as oil, an important input), which firms pass on to consumers as higher prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: During a period of unanticipated inflation, which group is most likely to benefit at the expense of creditors and fixed-income earners?
options: Savers holding cash deposits
Pensioners on a fixed monthly pension
Debtors, who repay loans with money of lower real purchasing power
Lenders who issued loans at fixed interest rates
questions.explanation: Inflation erodes the real value of money, so debtors benefit by repaying fixed-value loans with money that is worth less than when it was borrowed, at the expense of creditors and those on fixed incomes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Hyperinflation refers to a situation of
options: an extremely rapid and often accelerating rise in prices, severely eroding the value of money
zero change in the general price level
a mild and stable annual rise in prices of about 2%
a steady fall in prices over several years
questions.explanation: Hyperinflation describes an extremely high and typically rapidly accelerating inflation rate, which can destroy the value and usefulness of a currency within a short period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A sustained fall in the general price level (deflation) is most commonly caused by
options: a rapid rise in government spending
a rise in the price of imported raw materials
a significant and sustained fall in aggregate demand or contraction of the money supply
an increase in the minimum wage across the economy
questions.explanation: Deflation typically results from weak aggregate demand or a shrinking money supply, leading to falling prices as spending in the economy declines.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Persistent inflation undermines money's function as a
options: medium of exchange only
store of value, since the purchasing power of money held over time falls
legal tender in international trade
unit of account only
questions.explanation: Because inflation continuously erodes purchasing power, money becomes a less reliable store of value the longer it is held during inflationary periods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An economy experiencing simultaneously high inflation, high unemployment, and stagnant economic growth is said to be facing
options: deflation
stagflation
hyperinflation only
a balanced budget crisis
questions.explanation: Stagflation is the unusual combination of high inflation with high unemployment and low or stagnant output growth, difficult to resolve with conventional demand-management policy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The central bank's role as 'lender of last resort' means it
options: provides personal loans directly to individual citizens
only lends money to foreign governments
refuses to lend to any financial institution under any circumstance
lends to commercial banks facing severe liquidity shortages when no other source of funds is available
questions.explanation: As lender of last resort, the central bank provides emergency liquidity support to solvent commercial banks in crisis, helping to maintain stability in the banking system.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Which of the following is best classified as a non-bank financial institution?
options: The central bank issuing currency
An insurance company or pension fund administrator
A commercial bank accepting current account deposits
A merchant bank offering demand deposit accounts
questions.explanation: Non-bank financial institutions, such as insurance companies and pension fund administrators, mobilise and invest funds but do not accept demand deposits or create money like commercial banks.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Open market operations, as a tool of monetary policy, involve the central bank
options: printing new currency notes without limit
buying or selling government securities to influence the level of money supply in the economy
directly setting the prices of consumer goods
collecting personal income tax from citizens
questions.explanation: Open market operations involve the central bank buying or selling government bonds/securities in the open market to expand or contract the money supply and influence interest rates.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A commercial bank holds total deposits of N10 million, and the central bank sets the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) at 25%. The amount the bank can legally lend out (loanable funds) is
options: N2.5 million
N7.5 million
N10 million
N12.5 million
questions.explanation: Required reserves = 25% x N10m = N2.5m; the remaining N10m - N2.5m = N7.5m is available for the bank to lend out.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Merchant/discount houses differ from ordinary commercial banks mainly in that they
options: accept small personal savings deposits from the general public
issue the national currency
primarily provide short-term wholesale finance, bill discounting, and services to corporate clients rather than retail deposit-taking
are owned exclusively by the central bank
questions.explanation: Merchant and discount houses typically focus on short-term corporate and wholesale financial services (such as discounting bills), rather than accepting everyday retail deposits like commercial banks.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: One of the main functions of a stock exchange in an economy is to
options: facilitate the buying and selling of existing shares and help firms raise long-term capital by issuing new securities
act as the sole lender of last resort to commercial banks
collect value-added tax on behalf of government
set the country's minimum wage
questions.explanation: A stock exchange provides a marketplace for trading existing securities and enables companies to raise long-term capital by issuing new shares or bonds to investors.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A tax system in which the rate of tax increases as a taxpayer's income increases is called
options: a regressive tax
an indirect tax
a progressive tax
a proportional tax
questions.explanation: A progressive tax takes a larger percentage of income from higher-income earners than from lower-income earners, as the tax rate rises with income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Under a progressive tax system, the first N300,000 of income is taxed at 10% and the next N200,000 at 20%. For a taxpayer earning N500,000, the total tax payable is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An indirect tax, such as Value Added Tax (VAT), differs from a direct tax mainly because it
options: is levied on goods and services and its burden can be shifted, at least partly, from the seller to the buyer
is only paid by government agencies
is levied directly on income and cannot be shifted to another party
can never be included in the price of a good
questions.explanation: Indirect taxes are imposed on transactions (goods/services), and sellers can often shift some or all of the tax burden onto buyers through higher prices, unlike direct taxes on income or wealth.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Adam Smith's canons (principles) of taxation include all of the following EXCEPT
options: certainty
equity (ability to pay)
convenience of payment
maximisation of government secrecy
questions.explanation: Adam Smith's classical canons of taxation are equity, certainty, convenience, and economy; secrecy in government operations is not one of these recognised principles.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: When the demand for a good is very inelastic, an indirect tax imposed on that good will most likely result in the tax burden falling mainly on
options: consumers, since they are less responsive to the resulting price rise
no one, since inelastic goods cannot be taxed
producers only, regardless of demand elasticity
the government, since it must absorb the tax cost
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, consumers continue buying similar quantities even as price rises, allowing producers to pass most of the tax burden onto consumers through higher prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: An expansionary fiscal policy, used to stimulate a sluggish economy, typically involves the government
options: reducing the money supply through open market sales
raising interest rates sharply
increasing government spending and/or reducing taxes to boost aggregate demand
cutting government spending and raising taxes
questions.explanation: Expansionary fiscal policy aims to boost aggregate demand and economic activity by increasing government expenditure and/or cutting taxes, unlike contractionary policy, which does the opposite.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A good is priced at N5,000 before tax, and VAT is charged at 7.5%. The total price the consumer pays, including VAT, is
questions.explanation: VAT amount = 7.5% x 5,000 = N375; total price = 5,000 + 375 = N5,375.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Public debt owed by a government to lenders within its own country, denominated in local currency, is known as
options: a trade deficit
internal (domestic) debt
external (foreign) debt
a balance of payments surplus
questions.explanation: Internal (domestic) debt is owed to lenders within the country, usually in local currency, distinguishing it from external debt owed to foreign creditors or institutions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Economic growth differs from economic development in that economic growth refers mainly to
options: a quantitative increase in a country's real output (real GDP) over time, without necessarily improving welfare
the elimination of all forms of poverty
improvements in literacy, health, and income distribution
the balance of payments position of a country
questions.explanation: Economic growth is a narrower, quantitative measure (rise in real GDP/output), while economic development is a broader concept encompassing improvements in living standards, health, education, and equity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Country A can use one unit of labour to produce 10 units of cloth or 5 units of wine (opportunity cost of 1 wine = 2 cloth). Country B can use one unit of labour to produce 6 units of cloth or 6 units of wine (opportunity cost of 1 wine = 1 cloth). Based on comparative advantage, Country B should specialise in
options: cloth, since it has the lower opportunity cost in cloth
wine, since it has the lower opportunity cost of producing wine
both goods equally, since costs are identical
neither good, since it has no absolute advantage
questions.explanation: Country B's opportunity cost of producing wine (1 cloth) is lower than Country A's (2 cloth), so B has a comparative advantage in wine and should specialise in it, leaving cloth to Country A.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: The current account of a country's balance of payments primarily records
options: only foreign exchange reserve movements
trade in goods and services, plus income and current transfers
only long-term capital investment flows into the country
the sale of government bonds to foreign investors
questions.explanation: The current account records trade in visible goods and invisible services, along with primary income (e.g., investment income) and current transfers, distinct from the capital/financial account, which records investment and asset flows.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A tariff differs from an import quota mainly in that a tariff
options: bans the importation of a good entirely, unlike a quota
is a tax imposed on imported goods, while a quota is a direct physical limit on the quantity that may be imported
applies only to exported goods, not imports
is a physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported, while a quota is a tax
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax levied on imports (raising their price), whereas a quota directly restricts the physical quantity of a good that can be imported, regardless of price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A country's export price index is 120 and its import price index is 100. Its terms of trade is
options: 83.3, indicating unfavourable terms of trade
120, indicating favourable (improved) terms of trade
20, indicating a trade deficit
100, indicating unchanged terms of trade
questions.explanation: Terms of Trade = (Export Price Index / Import Price Index) x 100 = (120/100) x 100 = 120, a value above 100 indicating favourable terms of trade.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Devaluation of a currency differs from depreciation in that devaluation is
options: a market-driven fall in currency value under a floating exchange rate system
always caused by inflation alone
only possible when a country has no central bank
a deliberate, official reduction in the value of a currency under a fixed exchange rate regime, while depreciation occurs automatically under a floating regime
questions.explanation: Devaluation is a deliberate policy action by the monetary authorities to lower a currency's fixed exchange rate value, whereas depreciation is a market-determined fall in value under a floating exchange rate system.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Compared to the IMF, which focuses on short-term monetary stability and balance of payments support, the World Bank primarily focuses on
options: setting exchange rates for all its member countries
providing long-term loans and technical assistance for development projects in member countries
printing currency notes for developing nations
managing the day-to-day monetary policy of member states
questions.explanation: While the IMF addresses short-term balance of payments and monetary stability issues, the World Bank concentrates on financing long-term development projects such as infrastructure, health, and education.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Dumping, in international trade, refers to the practice of
options: imposing high tariffs on all imported goods
a country refusing to trade with any other nation
banning the export of a particular good
a firm selling goods in a foreign market at a price below cost or below its home market price, often to eliminate competition
questions.explanation: Dumping occurs when a firm exports goods at prices below their cost of production or below the price charged domestically, often used strategically to undercut competitors in the foreign market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Nigeria's post-independence National Development Plans were primarily designed to
options: fix permanent prices for all goods and services
eliminate the need for any future economic planning
exclusively fund military expenditure
provide medium-term frameworks for guiding economic growth, resource allocation, and infrastructural development
questions.explanation: Nigeria's National Development Plans set medium-term goals and priorities to guide public investment, resource allocation, and structural transformation of the economy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: A persistent balance of payments deficit is most commonly financed by
options: permanently banning all imports
drawing down foreign exchange reserves, borrowing from abroad, or securing IMF financial assistance
reducing the population through migration policy
increasing domestic tax rates on all citizens
questions.explanation: Countries facing a balance of payments deficit typically finance the shortfall by depleting foreign reserves, taking on foreign loans, or seeking support from international bodies such as the IMF.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.text: Third-degree price discrimination, commonly practised by monopolists, differs from first-degree price discrimination in that the seller
options: refuses to sell to any group with elastic demand
charges a single uniform price to all consumers regardless of group
charges different prices to distinct identifiable groups of consumers (such as students versus adults) based on differing group elasticities of demand
charges every individual consumer their own exact maximum willingness to pay
questions.explanation: Third-degree price discrimination segments the market into identifiable groups with different price elasticities and charges each group a different price, unlike first-degree discrimination, which targets each individual consumer's exact willingness to pay.
